title: Dubai's Job Crisis Deepens as Iran War Squeezes Indian and Migrant Workers Across the Gulf
excerpt: Construction freezes, tourism layoffs, and a UAE localization mandate are hitting millions of Indian workers, with over 15,000 seafarers still stranded near the Strait of Hormuz four months after the conflict began.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Over 15,000 Indian seafarers are stranded near the Strait of Hormuz due to ongoing conflict.
  • A new UAE localization mandate is freezing recruitment of South Asian laborers in government projects.
  • Dubai's tourism and construction sectors have laid off tens of thousands of workers since February.
  • Gulf-origin remittances to India dropped 12% in the March quarter, impacting household incomes.
Stranded Seafarers Crisis
›15,000+ Indian seafarers stranded near Strait of Hormuz.
›India advises against new crew voyages in the area.
›Complex rescue efforts due to scattered locations.
›Previous evacuations were more straightforward.
  • Over 15,000 Indian seafarers remain stranded on vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, with India advising new crews to avoid the waterway.
  • A UAE localization mandate imposed within weeks of the war requires one Emirati hire for every foreign worker on government projects, freezing recruitment of South Asian laborers.
  • Dubai's tourism, construction, and logistics sectors have shed tens of thousands of jobs since the conflict began in February.
  • Gulf-origin remittances to India declined 12 percent in the March quarter, threatening household incomes in states most dependent on Gulf earnings.

Four months after US and Israeli airstrikes on Iran triggered retaliatory attacks across the Gulf, the economic aftermath is falling hardest on the workers who built the region's skylines — and the vast majority of them are Indian.

More than half of Dubai's residents come from India. The Strait of Hormuz conflict has disrupted the economic model that drew them there: construction contracts are frozen, tourism revenues have collapsed, and a new UAE localization mandate has added a sharp labor-market bottleneck on top of the war's direct damage.

Stranded at Sea

More than 15,000 Indian seafarers remain trapped on vessels west of the Strait of Hormuz, according to Manoj Yadav, general secretary of the Forward Seamen's Union of India. India's maritime authority has issued an advisory urging new crews not to accept voyages through the waterway.

"We can stop the new sets of crews from joining in those areas. But what about those thousands of seafarers who are still trapped in those deadly seas and under the threat to their lives? What is the government doing to take them out?"

— Manoj Yadav, Forward Seamen's Union of India

The question has gone largely unanswered. While India has evacuated citizens from conflict zones before — most notably during the 2015 Yemen crisis — the current situation involves workers scattered across commercial shipping vessels rather than concentrated in a single port, making a coordinated rescue far more complex.

Construction Freeze

The UAE's construction sector, which employs hundreds of thousands of Indian workers in roles from site labor to project engineering, has been among the hardest hit. Rystad Energy estimates a $58 billion reconstruction bill across the region, but the work has barely begun.

Reconstruction is competing with Qatar's massive North Field gas project and Saudi-UAE gigaprojects for fabrication yards, engineering talent, and heavy-lift capacity, according to Engineering News-Record. Insurance premiums have surged, and many workers who returned to India during the peak of hostilities are reluctant to go back.

The UAE imposed a localization mandate within two weeks of the war's outbreak, requiring private firms on government-linked projects to employ one Emirati for every foreign worker. While the policy aims to fast-track Emirati employment, its immediate effect has been to freeze hiring of the migrant workforce that forms the backbone of Gulf construction.

"It's not helping," said Syed Farooq, managing director of Al Syed Staffing Solutions, describing the mandate's impact on a labor market already reeling from conflict disruption.

Tourism and Services Gutted

Dubai's tourism sector, which employed tens of thousands of Indian workers in hotels, restaurants, and retail, has seen sharp layoffs since the conflict began. The Burj Al Arab hotel and Dubai International Airport — the world's busiest — sustained damage during Iranian retaliatory strikes. Emergency alerts sent residents scrambling to shelters, and nearly 30,000 British nationals alone left the UAE in the immediate aftermath.

The Business and Human Rights Resource Centre has documented a pattern of deteriorating conditions for migrant workers across Gulf states since February: wage theft and delayed payments in construction, project cancellations in Kuwait, phone searches and restricted movement flagged by Human Rights Watch, and reports of unsafe working conditions intensifying month over month.

The Remittance Squeeze

For India, the Gulf crisis carries macroeconomic weight. Indian nationals in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, and Bahrain sent home roughly $35 billion in remittances in 2025, according to the World Bank. The Reserve Bank of India flagged remittance risk in its June financial stability report, noting that Gulf-origin transfers had declined 12 percent in the March quarter compared to the prior year.

A prolonged Gulf downturn would squeeze household incomes across Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, and Uttar Pradesh — the states most dependent on Gulf earnings. For many families in these regions, a monthly transfer from Dubai or Riyadh is the difference between stability and hardship.

What Comes Next

India's External Affairs Ministry has set up a crisis desk and issued travel advisories, but has stopped short of calling for a mass evacuation. The situation remains in flux: oil prices have stabilized above $90, construction tenders are slowly resuming in less-affected zones, and some airlines have begun restoring routes suspended during the peak of hostilities.

For the millions of Indians who went to the Gulf seeking opportunity, the calculation has fundamentally changed. The region that once offered a reliable path to middle-class earnings now carries risks that many workers and their families are unwilling to accept.

Impact on Employment
›UAE construction sector faces $58 billion reconstruction bill.
›Localization mandate requires one Emirati hire per foreign worker.
›Hiring freeze affects migrant workforce in construction.
›Insurance premiums have surged, complicating recovery.
Remittance Decline
›$35 billion in remittances sent to India from Gulf in 2025.

image_caption: Dubai's skyline was built largely by migrant labor from South Asia. Four months into the Iran war, construction freezes and a new localization mandate are hitting those workers hardest.
nri_angle: Over 3 million Indian nationals live and work in the Gulf states. A prolonged downturn threatens the roughly $35 billion in annual remittances that Gulf-based Indians send home to families across Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and Uttar Pradesh.
